title: How Standardized Patients Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain standardized patients (also called simulated or programmed patients): actors or lay people who portray patients so medical students can practice history-taking, diagnosis, and bedside manner. They cover the origins with USC neurologist Howard Barrow in the 1960s, slow adoption, the role's requirements (memorized character, consistent performance across about ten student encounters a day, feedback and grading), care actors for practicing physicians, unannounced standardized patients used as secret shoppers, and the male and female genitourinary teaching associates who teach intimate exams. The episode opens with tour dates and a Seinfeld tangent and closes with a listener email from a Vancouver listener.
topics: University of Pittsburgh standardized patient program

segments.title: Tour dates and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck read off their North American tour dates and benefit show details, then banter about a Miley Cyrus song and a Seinfeld episode featuring a standardized patient.

segments.title: History: Howard Barrow and early standardized patients
segments.summary: Howard Barrow, a USC neurologist, created standardized patients in the late 1950s and early 1960s after finding that graduates were unprepared for real patients. Paula Stillman independently had a similar idea in the early 1970s. Early newspaper coverage sensationalized the program and adoption came in the mid-1980s.

segments.title: Why bedside manner and history-taking matter
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why doctors need communication skills to diagnose patients, citing Valerie Former of the University of Pittsburgh on communication and medical error, and the need to balance empathy with clinical detachment.

segments.title: Definitions and how standardized patients work
segments.summary: Standardized patients are people who portray a patient with a set character profile, without a memorized script, and perform the same case for about ten students a day so that they can be graded consistently. Cases may be invented or based on real cases, sometimes matched by age, gender and ethnicity.

segments.title: Leslie Jamison's essay and patient motives
segments.summary: Leslie Jamison's essay The Empathy Exams describes her time as a standardized patient playing a character with grief-related seizures. The hosts discuss why people volunteer and the risk of hidden agendas, such as a patient who promoted alternative medicine.

segments.title: Qualifications, stamina and the role's demands
segments.summary: Standardized patients must be upbeat, comfortable with doctors, able to give feedback, and have a good memory, since they may perform up to ten sessions of about forty-five minutes each. The work is part-time and pays modestly, and there is little controlled trial evidence of its effectiveness.

segments.title: CPR and surgical simulator robots
segments.summary: Chuck recalls learning CPR and the hosts discuss how chest compressions are emphasized over breaths. They then describe expensive lifelike surgical simulators used to train surgeons, and a pickled serial killer head photo shared on Twitter.

segments.title: Recruiting and the pay of standardized patients
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the selectiveness of recruiting, the need for flexibility and direction from educators, and that the pay is modest enough that it is generally a part-time gig.

segments.title: Care actors
segments.summary: Care actors are used for practicing physicians who want to improve a specific skill, such as empathy or handling anger, and can repeat scenes on demand, unlike standardized patients used for early-stage students.

segments.title: Unannounced standardized patients
segments.summary: Unannounced standardized patients act as secret shoppers in hospitals and doctors' offices to rate the patient experience from start to finish.

segments.title: Male and female genitourinary teaching associates
segments.summary: Mike Manning, a male urogenital teaching associate, has done thousands of prostate exams for students, and Katie Patterson teaches gynecological exams. Paid roughly thirty-five to fifty dollars per student per day, they are trained to teach intimate exams under professional supervision. The hosts note that medical schools historically hired prostitutes for gynecological training.

segments.title: Closing pitch and listener email
segments.summary: The hosts close the standardized patient discussion with a pitch to listeners interested in the work, then read a listener email from Kaya, a South African who moved to Canada, thanking the hosts for company while living far from home.
